title: Graduation Party Planning Kit
subtitle: An open-house style graduation party, planned around the May and June Chicago crunch
intro: Graduation season is short and everyone books at once. This kit walks you from the first venue call to the last thank-you note, with food amounts, a photo table plan, a budget split, and a rain plan so the day stays about the graduate.

sections.heading: Planning Timeline
sections.note: Chicago-area graduation weekends fill up early. Start before the school year ends.

tasks: Pick two or three possible dates and check them against the school ceremony, relatives' travel, and other grads in your circle.
Choose open-house hours, such as 1 to 5 pm, so guests can drop in without a formal meal.
Set a total budget and decide who is contributing.
Reserve a backyard, park shelter, banquet room, or community space and ask what rentals are included.
Request a quote for a tent, tables, and chairs now, since May and June weekends go first.
Book the caterer, food truck, or taco bar vendor before their calendar fills.
Draft the guest list with a first, second, and maybe-if-room tier.
Order or design invitations and announcements.
Pick a color scheme tied to school colors or the graduate's plans.
Ask the graduate to pick the music, the cake flavor, and one thing they definitely want.
Ask a friend or relative to collect photos for the display.
Mail invitations with an RSVP date about two weeks before the party.
Confirm rental quantities for chairs, tables, linens, and any tent.
Order the cake or dessert table items.
Check local park or village rules on tents, amplified music, and street parking.
Plan a photo display and order any prints, banners, or yard signs.
Line up helpers for setup, serving, and cleanup.
Follow up with guests who have not replied.
Give the caterer or grocery store an estimated headcount.
Buy drinks, ice, paper goods, and serving utensils if self-catering.
Confirm the rental delivery window and who will be home to receive it.
Test the speaker, slideshow, or playlist.
Check the forecast every day and decide your rain plan by Wednesday.
Give final headcount to the caterer 7 to 10 days out if they ask for it.
Mow, weed, and clear the yard or tidy the venue entry.
Prepare a cooler plan: ice, extra coolers, and a spot out of the sun.
Print a simple schedule and a map or parking note for guests.
Pack a day-of kit with tape, scissors, trash bags, wipes, and extension cords.
Set up tables and chairs at least 2 hours before guests arrive.
Put food out in small batches to keep it fresh.
Greet guests and make sure the graduate gets a few moments with everyone.
Bag trash and recycling as you go.
Stack and ready rentals for pickup per your agreement.
Send thank-you notes within two weeks and note any gift tracking.

sections.heading: Planning Checklists
sections.note: Check items off as you go.

groups.title: Venue and Space
items: Decide indoor, outdoor, or both.
Estimate how many guests will be there at once (usually fewer than the full list).
Confirm access time for setup and the hard stop for cleanup.
Check restroom access and capacity.
Ask about parking, street permits, and neighbor notice.
Plan a shaded or covered area for food and older guests.

groups.title: Rentals
items: Seating for about 50 to 60 percent of guests at one time.
Cocktail or standing tables for mingling.
Banquet or six-foot tables for food, drinks, and desserts.
A separate table for gifts and cards, with a card box.
Tablecloths or linens in the party colors.
Tent or canopy sized for the food area plus seating.
Chafing dishes or warming equipment if serving hot food.
Plates, napkins, cutlery, and cups or glassware if not using disposables.

groups.title: Food and Drink
items: Choose a service style: buffet, stations, food truck, or drop-off trays.
Plan for dietary needs such as vegetarian, gluten-free, and nut allergies.
Order a cake or cupcakes and a small cutting cake if desired.
Plan nonalcoholic drinks first, then decide on beer or wine.
Arrange extra ice and coolers.
Label food with simple cards.

groups.title: Display and Decor
items: Photo timeline from baby photos to senior year.
Trophies, jerseys, art, and awards the graduate wants to show.
Cap and gown on a stand or in a clear display area.
A guest book or advice cards for the graduate.
Balloons, banner, and yard signs.
A memory jar or video recording station for guests.

groups.title: Day of
items: Assign someone to manage the cooler and drinks.
Assign a photographer or photo-taker for candid shots.
Put out hand sanitizer and a trash station.
Have a rain plan helper ready to move signs, tables, and food.
Collect gifts and cards in one secure spot.
Send leftovers home with relatives in disposable containers.

sections.heading: Food Amounts by Guest Count
sections.note: Rough guidelines for a 3 to 4 hour open house. Adjust for the time of day and your crowd.

sections.heading: Budget Split
sections.note: Typical shares of a graduation party budget. Use this as a starting point and adjust.

lines.tip: Open houses run lighter than a dinner, so consider grazing tables and a few quality hot items.
Water, lemonade, and soda go further than you expect.
Get quotes early. Tent prices in May and June are higher because demand is high.
Park shelters and community rooms are often the least expensive.
A cutting cake plus cupcakes can lower cost.
A printed photo timeline is a simple, personal centerpiece.
Digital invitations save money and are easy to update.
A speaker and playlist is often enough.
Keep a small cushion for last-minute needs like extra ice.

sections.heading: Display and Photo Table Plan
sections.note: A good display gives guests something to talk about.

groups.title: Photos
items: Gather 20 to 40 photos spanning toddler through senior year.
Scan old prints at 300 dpi or take clear photos of them.
Print at 4x6 or 5x7 and group them by era.
Use clips on twine, a corkboard, or foam board so nothing gets damaged.
Add short captions with ages or grades.

groups.title: Memorabilia
items: Pick three to five meaningful items instead of everything.
Include team photos, awards, and favorite projects.
Display the diploma cover or a framed program.
Use risers or boxes to add height.
Keep fragile items away from the food table.

groups.title: Interactive Touches
items: Advice cards and a box for the graduate to read later.
A slideshow loop on a laptop or tablet.
A photo booth corner with a banner and props.
A map pin board for where the graduate is headed next.

sections.heading: Rain and Weather Plan
items: Decide your go or no-go for the tent by the Wednesday before the party and share it with your rental company.
Ask your rental company about tent sidewalls, anchoring, and weights if the ground is hard or you cannot stake.
Choose an indoor fallback such as a garage, basement, or community room and map where the food would go.
Plan for a hot afternoon with shade, fans, water stations, and cold towels.
Chicago can swing from cool and damp to hot in the same week in May and June, so keep a few umbrellas and light layers handy.
Use heavy items, not light signs, to hold down tablecloths and banners on windy days.
Keep your food table in the shade and use warming or cooling equipment that matches the weather.
Tell guests where to park and where to go if the weather changes.
Have a plan for wet chairs: towels and a way to dry them quickly.

sections.heading: Questions to Ask Vendors
items: What is included in your open-house packages, and how many people does each portion size serve?
Do you provide serving staff, chafing dishes, and utensils, or do I supply them?
What is the minimum order, and how far out is the final headcount due?
When will rentals arrive and when will they be picked up?
Are tent anchoring options available for grass, patio, or driveway?
What is your policy if the weather forces a change within 48 hours?
Is there a cleaning or damage fee for rentals?
Can you deliver on a Saturday morning in May or June, and what is the delivery window?

sections.heading: Party Worksheet
sections.note: Fill this out and keep it on the fridge.
